title: Brian Eno Wants to Show You His Creative Process │ Exclaim!
text:
School of Song has hosted songwriting classes and creative programs with a bunch of high-profile, beloved songwriters — Adrianne Lenker, Robin Pecknold and Phil Elverum, to name a few — but their upcoming January program is a real doozy.
The legendary multi-hyphenate Brian Eno will be teaching the upcoming program, "[guiding] students through his multifaceted relationship to the creative process, sharing many techniques and practices he has developed throughout his career."
Eno has been making music and art in various forms for decades, and he's inarguably changed the face of popular music a few times. His most recent album, ForeverAndEverNoMore was released back in October 2022, and he has recently written his second book, What Art Does, co-authored with Bette A., which is set to arrive in the new year.
The workshop "will cover a wide range of topics related to music making and is geared towards anyone interested in furthering their musical practice." A selection of workshop topics topics includes: The Role of Surrender, Avant Gardening, Creating a Compelling Sonic World, Oblique Strategies, and Should Music Still Be Called Music?
Of the program, Eno said, "I'm looking forward to the chance to properly articulate some ideas about the creative process that have been fermenting over the last 50 years. To be able to do this with some fresh young minds and imaginations was a chance that I couldn't refuse."
The workshop will include four lectures, taking place on Sundays — January 5, 12, 19 and 26 at 12 p.m. PT (3 p.m. ET). Each lecture is approximately 75 minutes, with the first class lasting two hours to include a live in-class writing exercise. The course will also include hour-long Q&As on Wednesdays — January 8, 15 and 22 at 12 p.m. PT (3 p.m. ET). The program will run you $160, and the deadline to sign up is January 4, 11:59 p.m. PT. Recorded lectures will be available and sent out afterward for anyone unable to attend at those times.
You can sign up here.

title: The Discreet Artistry of Brian Eno - Kyle's Newsletter
text:
The Discreet Artistry of Brian Eno
In a time that could use more playfulness and calm, I hope the music of Brian Eno brings you this
Introduction
What genre of music might one be capable of listening to for hundreds of hours, without growing tired of its presence? What sounds and textures are capable of drawing a listener into captivating new worlds one day, then playing the part of ignorable background noise the next? What creative techniques and approaches promote the development of some of popular music’s most recognizable albums? Surely the mastermind behind such achievements would be praised for their unprecedented artistic contributions.
Throughout history there are certain figures who leave an outsized imprint on their cultural zeitgeist, or spirit of the time—Brian Eno is no exception. Born May 15, 1948 in Suffolk, England, Eno first came to prominence in 1971 as keyboardist of the band Roxy Music.1 Although the band would come to greatly influence later New Wave groups such as Duran Duran, Depeche Mode, and Talking Heads with their “Warholian fusion of pop and art,” Eno would depart Roxy Music in 1973 to embark on a solo career.2 His earliest solo works of experimental, progressive rock albums utilized tape-echo and tape-delay techniques, before evolving into a more minimalist approach with Discreet Music (1975) and Ambient 1: Music for Airports (1978), two albums which would become synonymous with the ambient genre he pioneered.3
Throughout his career, he collaborated with and produced music for an impressive list of artists, including Devo, Ultravox, David Bowie, Talking Heads, David Byrne, Robert Fripp, U2, Laurie Anderson, John Cale, Paul Simon, Coldplay, and James Blake. Educated at Ipswich Art School and receiving his Diploma in Fine Art from the Winchester School of Art in the late 1960s, Eno has cultivated a parallel career as a visual artist experimenting with light, video, and generative themes across his music, installations and physical creations.1 On top of all this, and in tune with his affinity for environmental sound, he’s held a consistent presence in the environmental movement space as a founding member of multiple activist organizations.4
So how does such a varied individual—someone famously known to call himself a “non-musician”—come to possess an unparalleled position in the history of both popular and experimental music, and the art world at large? A position so revered that he was asked to design a piece of audio as ubiquitous as the Microsoft Windows 95 start up sound.
Popular music has long been dominated by Western countries, particularly the US and the UK. While a global analysis of the following sort would yield significant insight, my own musical interests and gaps in knowledge discourage me from making any rhetorical argument outside of the Western tradition. That said, my thesis is thus:
Through his experimental and open-minded philosophy of creativity and art, his trailblazing ambient works, and the connections and collaborations he fostered producing legendary musical acts, I will illustrate why Brian Eno is the most influential figure in Western music of the last 50 years.
Eno’s Philosophy of Art
Feelings and Play
“Play is how children learn. Art is how adults play.”
This is the thesis to Brian Eno and Bette Adriaanse’s 2025 book What Art Does: An Unfinished Theory.5 In this small, colorful, playful book, the two attempt to communicate a theory of what are is, what art does, and why we need it. The first part is simple: art is everything humans do outside of the immediate need or function of something.
They give the example of a cup. A functional cup needs to hold liquid, and it needs to be drinkable from. But a cup doesn’t need a handle and beautiful designs on it—these are artistic, stylistic additions. From this definition, nearly everything can be viewed as art, which itself is an uplifting reinterpretation from the pretentious, exclusive tendencies often associated with certain forms of art.
We humans go through this extra effort on ‘non-functional activities’ because what art does is make feelings happen. Art allows us to create new worlds in which we’re able to experiment with feelings—feelings which lead to thoughts about what type of person we want to be—in a safe environment without serious consequences.5 Eno expands on this idea in an interview with Zane Lowe of Apple Music:
“Adults are playing through art. I think that’s where we play. We carry on playing, but we call it art, and we call it going to the theatre, or we call it getting a new album, or whatever we call it. But I think that’s still the same instinct. To see what other worlds are like, to see what it’s like to be in this place and what feelings we have from it.”6
In this notion of play driving the artistic impulse, there is little room for strict rules and unwavering routines. It is this dedication to creative freedom, orchestrating a playground for adults, that, once set in motion, sets the groundwork for Eno’s exceptional artistic impact.
In fact, Eno invented “Oblique Strategies” specifically to avoid habits and ingrained ways of thinking. Developed in partnership with painter Peter Schmidt and “modelled philosophically on the ancient Chinese I Ching or Book of Changes,” Oblique Strategies is a deck of cards each presenting an aphorism to assist in the creative process.1 The cryptic, vague messages vary: “Honor thy mistake as a hidden intention,” “Disconnect from desire,” and “Retrace your steps” are just a few examples.1 In the book Brian Eno: His Music and the Vertical Sound of Color, author Eric Tamm writes:
Bowie and Eno used the deck of Oblique Strategies extensively in the making of “Heroes”…When they began work on “Sense of Doubt,” each pulled out a card and kept it a secret: “It was like a game. We took turns working on it, he’d do one overdub and I’d do the next. The idea was that each was to observe his Oblique Strategy as closely as he could. And as it turned out they were entirely opposed to one another. Effectively mine said, ‘Try to make everything as similar as possible,’ ... and his said ‘Emphasize differences.’”1
To Eno, simply repeating the success of previous artworks is perhaps the greatest sin an artist can commit. From the Oblique Strategies above, one can decipher the non-linear manner in which Eno believes art reveals itself to the maker. The process is about curiosity and wonder, what Tamm calls one of Eno’s primary assets: “He never seems to stray far from a sense of the inherent mystery of the world, and that sense of mystery excites and motivates him.”1
“Not a musician”
In Tamm’s thorough account of Eno’s early career, he unravels the frequent assertion—even the romantic mythology—that Eno is “not a musician.”
“Eno is in fact a talented and versatile, if intuitive and marginally skilled, multi-instrumentalist: he has played synthesizers, piano, organ, other electronic keyboards, electric guitar, electric bass guitar…and assorted traditional and ‘found’ percussion instruments such as ashtrays and flexible plastic pipes.”1
That being said, Eno isn’t known to be an expert at any musical instrument (aside from the synthesizer), a fact which I argue has proven advantageous to his creative output.
In the thought-provoking book Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialist World, David Epstein describes InnoCentive, a company centered on the notion that outsiders can often solve problems that’ve held specialists stumped. The idea goes that as our expertise grows in an area, our thinking becomes constrained by patterns of routine thinking, as if stuck in a box. This “box” often aids us in specific, familiar tasks, but poses limitations with more varied, complex problems.
“InnoCentive works in part because, as specialists become more narrowly focused, ‘the box’ is more like Russian nesting dolls. Specialists divide into subspecialties, which soon divide into sub-subspecialties. Even if they get outside the small doll, they may get stuck inside the next, slightly larger one.”7
But sometimes all it takes is someone with a fresh pair of eyes and general knowledge across a broad range, rather than exceptional depth in one specific topic. This is precisely what Eno brings to any creative environment: the freedom and inspiration to approach a project in a novel way, thereby unlocking new ways of thinking and creating.
Perhaps surprisingly, Eno never received any formal training in music theory and, in 1985, claimed to hardly listen to records at all. Tamm writes about this exchange with an interviewer in which Eno answers the question of the deliberateness of abstaining from music:
“I don’t think about it. I don’t have a record player, funnily enough. I think life’s too short to listen to records, at the moment. Well, I do listen to some things, but I usually like to listen to the same thing over and over for months…I’m quite happy to accept that I don’t know most of what’s going on in the world of music. I never have done. You have a choice when you get interested in culture. You have a choice of trying to absorb it all, the American style of ‘doing the sights’ in two days, or else you can just decide: ‘I’ll stay in this one place, because I like it here anyway, and I’ll really understand this. I’ll really find out about it.’ That’s what I do.”
By listening to fewer pieces of music more frequently, Eno is answering what musician Jon Hassell once said is the most important question we can ask ourselves: What is it that I really like?5 Through depth of listening, Eno sharpens his affinities for certain sounds and textures, while not being influenced externally by the standards and expectations of the broader music industry.
Where Do Ideas and Creativity Come From?
As much as this analysis is meant to explain what sets Eno apart, he increasingly refutes the notion of the individual genius. In his conception of feeling, thinking, and artistic creation, he’s created the word “scenius” to describe the way in which ideas incubate within layers of ecological support.
This concept is extrapolated upon in What Art Does:
“Individuals articulate ideas but it’s communities that produce, support and nurture them. A single flower is the product of a whole landscape. Just as there is no such thing as a self-made flower, there’s no such thing as a self-made human.”5
While we’re all capable of passively receiving ideas from our environment, it is those with the keenest capacity for attention that are able to most effectively harness and subjectively articulate the societal moment, redirecting it through unforgettable works of art. And yet it is this same attention, perhaps more than any other intrinsic human resource, that is being threatened by technological modernity, with its clandestine algorithms pulling our focus away from where we want it: on those things we truly like and want to learn more about. In this way, Eno’s philosophies extend beyond the confines of intentional artistic creation, into the realm of navigating the distractions of everyday life.
Early Solo Career, Discreet Music, and Generative Art
Soon after departing Roxy Music, Eno began releasing solo and collaborative “progressive rock” albums, utilizing unique tape-echo, tape-delay, and other experimental layers of sound. His first album No Pussyfooting, in partnership with Robert Fripp, reached the Top 30 in Britain.3 In other of his early solo works, including Here Come the Warm Jets (1974), Taking Tiger Mountain (By Strategy) (1974) and Another Green World (1975), listeners can observe the shift from rock to more contemplative, minimalist sounds for which Eno would come to be known.
“Since I have always preferred making plans to executing them, I have gravitated towards situations and systems that, once set into operation, could create music with little or no intervention on my part. That is to say, I tend towards the roles of planner and programmer, and then become an audience to the results.”9
This quote is Eno’s introduction to the liner notes (text printed on a sleeve of a record) of Discreet Music (1975). Arising from roughly a decade of Eno’s experimentations with the “long delay echo system,” Discreet Music utilized an apparatus that, once set in motion, produced a work of self-generation.9
“Having set up this apparatus, my degree of participation in what it subsequently did was limited to (a) providing an input (in this case, two simple and mutually compatible melodic lines of different duration stored on a digital recall system) and (b) occasionally altering the timbre of the synthesizer’s output by means of a graphic equalizer.”9
In this work Eno gladly accepts a passive role, avoiding “the tendency to play the artist by dabbling and interfering.”9 Eno’s fascination with Eastern philosophy encouraged him to avoid the human inclination to shape and control reality, instead revealing himself and his creativity to the rhythms of the universe, like a jellyfish adrift at sea. In becoming the audience to your own work, one can better observe the direction in which the art wants to go, which is often contrary to what one originally has in mind.
Eno would continue his explorations of generative art composition in the album Generative Music 1 (1996), the installation 77 Million Paintings (2006), and a 2024 documentary directed by Gary Hustwit titled Eno. In this audio-visual experience, no two viewings of the documentary are identical thanks to its algorithmic compiling from more than 30 hours of interviews with Eno and 500 hours of archival footage.10 And while the notion of generative art may associate the mind with anxiety of A.I.’s expanding presence, there is something to be said about the human intention and personality behind these types of artworks.
Memorably, Eno depicts—or, I should say, some versions of the ever-changing film depict—a story of David Bowie. During his Isolar–1976 Tour, while experiencing severe physical and mental deterioration from his cocaine addiction, the pop icon was only able to listen to the calming, repetitive drones of Discreet Music on repeat while traveling in between shows.11 This is a testament to the alternative worlds provided by ambient music, perhaps saving Bowie from what could have been even further decline and a shortened career.
My original inspiration for an article about Eno’s artistic approach came the night I first watched the documentary, staying up contemplating the idea of playfulness. With the energetic fervor that accompanies new favorite songs, I played Spinning Away and Strange Overtones on repeat while playing Yahtzee with my cat (I won)—my thoughts evolving from artistry, to how beautiful it is that we play simple games just to pass the time.
Creation of Ambient Music Genre
By the late 1970s, having just collaborated on multiple historic albums with David Bowie on his “Berlin Trilogy,” as well as the Talking Heads, Eno began to feel “personally less drawn to rock as a medium…that he had taken rock as far as he wanted to go with it.”1 In 1982, Eno said:
“Effectively, what I’ve done is abandoned rock music, because, for me, rock isn’t capable of producing that spiritual quality anymore. And, in fact, I don’t really hear anything at the moment that disputes my feeling.”1
And again in 1983:
“I don’t get the feeling of discovering new worlds from pop music that I used to get, just of being shown old ones over and over. One automatically thinks that’s because I’m getting old, which is true but that doesn’t mean one is getting jaded. I still get feeling and experience from other areas, but not rock.”1
Those other areas had become increasingly minimalist, resulting in his four-volume Ambient series, particularly the groundbreaking 1978 work Ambient 1: Music for Airports.
Eno had long been influenced by minimalism—a highly tonal genre of music represented by repetition, simple patterns, and spatiality—and the innovators John Cage, La Monte Young, Terry Reilly, and Steve Reich. As he was concurrently moving further away from the repetitive nature of rock, Eno set out to define a new genre—perhaps more of a theory, in his conception of it.1 Eric Tamm writes:
“For Eno, minimalism represents the most significant and potentially fruitful aesthetic point of departure in the 20th century—a new musical meta-idea, so to speak, which promises untold riches not simply in the development of compositional techniques, but in the development of new ways of listening.”
In the liner notes to Music for Airports—for many the exemplar of Ambient Music, with its frequent lack of drums, pulse or vocals—Eno expands on his pioneering undertaking. In response to Muzak—the form of music designed by Muzak Inc. in the fifties as an environmental background element, using “familiar tunes arranged and orchestrated in a lightweight and derivative manner”—Eno set out to create environmental music that doesn’t provoke a dismissive attitude from listeners. In the notes to the album Eno writes:
“An ambience is defined as an atmosphere, or a surrounding influence, a tint. My intention is to produce original pieces ostensibly (but not exclusively) for particular times and situations with a view to building up a small but versatile catalogue of environmental music suited to a wide variety of moods and atmospheres…And whereas their intention is to `brighten’ the environment by adding stimulus to it (thus supposedly alleviating the tedium of routine tasks and levelling out the natural ups and downs of the body rhythms) Ambient Music is intended to induce calm and a space to think.”12
These liner notes, included on many of Eno’s key works, can be viewed as essays, an opportunity for an artist primarily working in the medium of sound to express his philosophies through language, which is purposely absent from much of his ambient catalogue. The final paragraph from this essay speaks of Ambient Music accommodating “many levels of listening attention without enforcing one in particular,” and closes with perhaps the most famous, graspable koan of ambient theory:
“It must be as ignorable as it is interesting.”
He derived the term Ambient Music to differentiate himself from the pallid, “canned” music to come before. Inherent to his entire philosophy is the desire to bring listeners in closer relationship with their environment, a type of music without sharp boundaries, something that “fades out into the rest of the world’s noises around you.”13
Of all places and activities that is asking to be lifted from its banal, chaotic, stress-inducing reality, and made to be more of a spiritual experience—does anything meet this call more than an airport and the (often terrifying) experience of flying? In this effort, Eno is admitting to the belief that we, collective society, deserve more meaningful music in the shared places that we live, work, and congregate. There exists a selflessness in this effort that lives outside the bounds of musical success, profit, recognition, and all the rest—one ultimately rooted in the collective over the individual.
The legacy of Ambient Music has shaped and given a platform for later notable ambient artists including Aphex Twin, Stars of the Lid, Eluvium, and Tim Hecker. Expanding out from the standard Ambient category are other genres such as Lo-Fi, Chillwave, and other instrumental sub-genres associated with themes of calm, relaxation, contemplation, and deep thinking—not to mention the application of ambient sounds and textures across all forms of modern music.
Significance in Popular Music
Throughout this analysis of Brian Eno’s impact, we’ve already come across examples of his collaboration and production with artists Roxy Music, David Bowie, and Talking Heads. It’s difficult to know exactly what knobs he may have turned, or which sound distortions and tape-delay effects he may have employed, but the simple fact of his association with the names already mentioned and those to come, and his presence for the creation of career-defining songs and albums, speaks to his creative influence.
And yet, the previously explained notion that Eno isn’t an expert musician suggests that one’s mind—their imagination and playfulness in the approach—shouldn’t be considered an instrument of musicianship. This myth, too, will be unraveled by the end of this essay. But let us first analyze a handful of prominent examples of Eno’s production, uncovering what it is he actually brings to the musical table.
Roxy Music
With Roxy Music, Eno’s greatest addition was that of the synthesizer, an instrument he’d never touched until one day, helping the band with some demo tapes, he conjured sounds so impressive that the band asked him to join on the spot. “I’m very good with technology. I always have been, and with machines in general. They seem to me not threatening like other people find them, but a source of great fun and amusement, like grown up toys really.”1
David Bowie
Alongside David Bowie for his “Berlin Trilogy”, Eno’s fingerprints are clearly audible in the song “Warszawa” with “piano drones and organ-like synthesizer tones,” also co-authoring the rock-anthem “Heroes” and providing synthesizers, keyboards, guitar treatments, and other unusual textures across the album.1
Talking Heads
In his three-album tenure with the Talking Heads, essentially operating as “a ghost member of the band, somewhat in the manner of the Beatles’ producer George Martin in the late 1960s,” Eno possessed considerable artistic sway.1 Tamm writes this about his influence: “Particularly striking aspects of the development of Talking Heads’ musical style during the Eno years were the simplification of harmonic materials and the increasingly pointillistic nature of the rhythms. In many of the songs on Remain In Light, one or two chords provide the harmonic underpinning for an ever-shifting array of percussive and melodic events.”1
David Byrne
Eno and Talking Heads frontman David Byrne connected so well they went on to collaborate multiple times, most prominently with the albums My Life in the Bush of Ghosts (1981) and Everything That Happens Will Happen Today (2008). WithMy Life in the Bush of Ghosts—the title of a book by Nigerian novelist Amos Tutuola—Eno aimed to create “fourth world music,” what he defined as “music that is done in sympathy with and with consciousness of music of the rest of the world, rather than just with Western music or just with rock music.”1 The album relied heavily on sampled voices from sources all around the world: a San Francisco radio host, the Lebanese singer Dunya Yusin, a sermon by Reverend Paul Morton, the Egyptian singer Samira Tewfik, and traditional Quran chanting, among others.1
While some critics believed the album succeeded in depicting a “pluralistic, world-wide contemporary culture of cultures knit together,” others raised questions about cultural imperialism and artistic appropriation.1 Jono Podmore reported on the topic of unfair audio sampling, summarizing their take in the following:
“I’d say this album is a case of appropriation gone right…Eno and Byrne were merely blundering their way into making a beautiful collection of tunes. No more and no less. Despite the apparent conscious ignorance of its creators, despite their colonial privilege, there are moments of profound cross-cultural beauty on this album…Yes—there is a background of direct theft, of imperialism, of colonialism behind My Life In The Bush Of Ghosts. But there has to be a case for quality, for bringing the art of other cultures into the mainstream, and for the validity of art beyond the important, but ultimately mundane, social restraints of respect and decency. This album makes that case, over and over again.”13
U2
Following the acclaim of their first two albums, U2 requested Eno for the recording of The Unforgettable Fire “to be changed unrecognizably,” as Bono told Eno.15 Embracing this open-ended invitation, Eno aimed to disrupt their typical routines and to steer the band toward spontaneous creation and the unknown. In credence to this purpose, Eno secretly recorded Adam Clayton and the Edge jamming, a piece that would ultimately become the instrumental track “4th of July.” Another story goes that Eno, continuing on to produce U2’s masterpiece The Joshua Tree, attempted to erase the entire saved recording of “Where the Streets Have No Name,” convinced that “sometimes destroying and rebuilding yields a better result than endless tinkering.”15 Eno “created a playground for U2 to experiment in,” helping them navigate creative roadblocks and overcome the pressures of merely repeating for formula of past successes.15
Coldplay
Coldplay’s 2008 magnum opus Viva La Vida or Death and All His Friends— winning a Grammy for Best Rock Album and cemented Coldplay’s status as one of the most influential bands of the 21st century—wouldn’t exist without Eno’s presence. “Building on Coldplay’s natural ability for melodic music-making, Eno emboldened the group by implementing his trademark use of soundscapes and ambient texture,” a prescient calculation in sync with the coming trajectory of alt-rock.16 Eno also inserted an overarching ground rule: that every song had to sound different than the others, leading to wildly varying songs each evoking “a different aspect of humanity—ranging from love (‘Lovers In Japan’) to war (‘Death and All His Friends’) to politics (‘Violet Hill’) to lust (‘Yes’) to loss (‘Viva La Vida’) to innocence (‘Strawberry Swing’).”16
Relationship with Fred Again..
To the writer of this analysis, one collaboration—really a friendship of reciprocal mentorship—stands out among the rest. As I endeavor to convince the reader of Brian Eno’s status as the most influential figure in Western music throughout the last half century, Fred Again.. (born Frederick John Philip Gibson) is attempting his own takeover of the crown in the electronic and popular music genres of the 2020s, having already secured a Brit Award in 2020 for British Producer of the Year.
Eno met the young producer when Fred was sixteen years of age, having been invited to join the choir group of which Eno was a member. Since then, the two have continually learned from one another, officially collaborating on the underrated joint-album Secret Life (2023). In an interview with Zane Lowe, Fred had this to say about Eno’s influence:
“The way in which his mind works, I don’t think a sixteen-year-old is primed to fully appreciate…but I think, in one word, it’s because he’s a kid. And in a way that is just so rare and so admirable, he’s retained this childish, wide-eyed fascination with things.”17
But where many mentor figures would simply accept such respect and admiration as the natural dynamic of two artists from different generations, too-often a one-way hierarchy of influence, Eno returns the compliment in a different interview:
“I think of Fred as my mentor as well. In that I learned so much about contemporary music from watching him working. You know, when I first worked with Fred, I could see he was brilliant. It’s very clear. He’s a very, very sensitive and good artist. And I was very impressed by that. I didn’t really understand a lot of what he was doing. It took me quite a while to think, ‘Oh my gosh this is really a new idea about how you can make music.’ So I learned a lot from him. It’s a two-way relationship, you know. I mean, I’m very flattered to be called a mentor of someone whose work I like a lot, but actually, it worked both ways around. I started listening to music differently when I watched how Fred was making it.”6
What is interesting about Eno and Fred’s relationship is not necessarily in the music they’ve made together, but in the comments depicted above regarding the way in which they perceive of and influence one another. Fred Again.. makes electronic music for kids and young adults seeking meaning out of music, dancing, and relationships. Already a massively successful producer, Fred began to attain further notoriety for his solo work in April 2021 with the release of Actual Life 1. In this album—along with the subsequent Actual Life 2 and Actual Life 3—Fred titles each track after the friend, stranger, or viral clip of whomever he’s sampled in the song itself. At this time, roughly a year into the Covid-19 pandemic, it was precisely these themes of personal relationship and human interaction that listeners were missing and longing for—typified by the song “Maria (we’ve lost dancing).”
Whether Fred is headlining a massive Coachella crowd, or sustaining unimaginably high levels of energy and good vibes in his iconic Boiler Room set, or simply making music with his friends and family, there is an ever-present reality that nothing is being taking too seriously. There is nobody in the music industry who more vividly displays the fun they are having, the feelings at the root of the creative experience, than Fred Again… It is fair to say that through his mentorship with Eno, or Fred’s own spirited personality, or some combination of the two, he is manifestly living out the artistic philosophy of Brian Eno, modern music’s great visionary.
Conclusion
I suppose this is where I admit my bias, that I am indeed the one capable of listening to the same ambient tracks for hundreds of hours. In 2025, my Spotify Wrapped recorded 80+ hours of Discreet Music—more specifically, the first song of the album which is thirty minutes of repetitive, atmospheric synthesizer tones and drones. Music for Airports and the album LUX are not far behind.
As far as this singular listener is concerned, Eno has succeeded in creating alternative worlds in which it feels safe to feel, whatever the emotion brought on by the day. On a regular basis my evenings wind down with one or another ambient albums, as I stretch on the carpeted floor, play with the pets, or explore the muted, swirling colors of the inside of my eyelids.
Brian Eno’s influence cannot be measured solely by the albums he produced, the genres pioneered, or the artists whose careers he reshaped—though these achievements alone would secure his place in history. His deeper contribution lies in how he has taught new generations of artists and listeners to pay attention: to feelings, to environments, and to one another. Whether through ambient music that creates new worlds and aids existing ones, production methods that prioritize play over control, or philosophical frameworks that dissolve the myth of the solitary genius, Eno consistently redirects focus away from dominance and toward relationship.
Across sixty years of creation, Eno has demonstrated that art is not merely an object to be consumed but a system to be inhabited—one that can hold multiple modes of listening, thinking, and being. His work resists urgency, offering instead spaces of calm, curiosity, and emergence. In an era increasingly defined by distraction and acceleration, this may be his most enduring legacy.
The continued relevance of Eno’s ideas suggests that his philosophy is not bound to a particular sound or generation. Rather, it endures as an ethic: that creativity flourishes through openness, feelings, and play. In this sense, Brian Eno stands not only as one of modern music’s most influential figures, but as one of its most generous.

title: Creative Practice Tips from Brian Eno — Think Jar Collective
text:
Creative Practice Tips from Brian Eno
Current neuroscience research confirms what creatives intuitively know about being innovative: that it usually happens in the shower. After focusing intently on a project or problem, the brain needs to fully disengage and relax in order for a “Eureka!” moment to arise. It’s often the mundane activities like taking a shower, driving, or taking a walk that lure great ideas to the surface. Composer Steve Reich, for instance, would ride the subway around New York when he was stuck.
Science journalist Jonah Lehrer, referencing a landmark neuroscience study on brain activity during innovation, writes:
“The relaxation phase is crucial. That’s why so many insights happen during warm showers. … One of the surprising lessons of this research is that trying to force an insight can actually prevent the insight.”
The ebb and flow of concentrated focus and total disengagement has been a subject of particular interest to the composer, musician, and producer Brian Eno (U2, Talking Heads, Roxy Music). Drawing on interviews from throughout Eno’s career, Eric Tamm’s book, Brian Eno: His Music and The Vertical Sound of Color, delves deeply into Eno’s “creative process.” Eno himself calls it:
...a practice of some kind ... It quite frequently happens that you’re just treading water for quite a long time. Nothing really dramatic seems to be happening. … And then suddenly everything seems to lock together in a different way. It’s like a crystallization point where you can’t detect any single element having changed. There’s a proverb that says that the fruit takes a long time to ripen, but it falls suddenly ... And that seems to be the process.
While neuroscience hasn’t yet been able to develop a foolproof scientific system to spark creativity, an artistic practice, if developed, can grease the wheels for more frequent and higher quality creative moments. As Eno puts it:
“The point about working is not to produce great stuff all the time, but to remain ready for when you can.”
He continues:
"There’s no point in saying, ‘I don’t have an idea today, so I’ll just smoke some drugs.’ You should stay alert for the moment when a number of things are just ready to collide with one another... The reason to keep working is almost to build a certain mental tone, like people talk about body tone. You have to move quickly when the time comes, and the time might come very infrequently – once or twice a year, or even less."
Craft, he says, “enables you to be successful when you’re not inspired.”
He goes on:
"The difficulty of always feeling that you ought to be doing something is that you tend to undervalue the times when you’re apparently doing nothing, and those are very important times. It’s the equivalent of the dream time, in your daily life, times when things get sorted out and reshuffled. If you’re constantly awake work-wise you don’t allow that to happen. One of the reasons I have to take distinct breaks when I work is to allow the momentum of a particular direction to run down, so that another one can establish itself."
Throughout his career, Eno has used a grab bag of tools to assist the creative process.
“There are lots of ways that you can interfere with it and make it more efficient.”
Freeform capture. Grab from a range of sources without editorializing. According to Tamm, one of Eno’s tactics “involves keeping a microcassette tape recorder on hand at all times and recording any stray ideas that hit him out of the blue – a melody, a rhythm, a verbal phrase.” He’ll then go through and look for links or connections, something that can form the foundation for a new piece of music.
Blank state. Start with new tools, from nothing, and toy around. For example, Eno approaches this by entering the recording studio with no preconceived ideas, only a set of instruments or a few musicians and “just dabble with sounds until something starts to happen that suggests a texture.” When the sound texture evokes a memory or emotion that impression then takes over in guiding the process.
Deliberate limitations. Before a project begins, develop specific limitations. Eno’s example: “this piece is going to be three minutes and nineteen seconds long and it’s going to have changes here, here and here, and there’s going to be a convolution of events here, and there’s going to be a very fast rhythm here with a very slow moving part over the top of it.”
Opposing forces. Sometimes it’s best to generate a forced collision of ideas. Eno would “gather together a group of musicians who wouldn’t normally work together.” Dissimilar background and approaches can often evoke fresh thinking.
Creative prompts. In the ‘70s Eno developed his Oblique Strategies cards, a series of prompts modeled to disrupt the process and encourage a new way of encountering a creative problem. On the cards are statements and questions like: “Would anybody want it?” “Try faking it!” “Only a part, not the whole.” “Work at a different speed.” “Disconnect from desire.” “Turn it upside down.” “Use an old idea.” These prompts are a method of generating specifics, which most creatives respond favorably to.
In the end, don’t underestimate your personal feelings about a project. Eno states: “Nearly all the things I do that are of any merit at all start off as just being good fun.”Further reading on related subjects

title: Video: Brian Eno on cowboys, creativity and surrender — Think Jar Collective
text:
Video: Brian Eno on cowboys, creativity and surrender
Brian Eno is one of the rare creative geniuses that allows people a glimpse into their creative process. Few artists are candid about how they approach creativity and so when you hear someone sharing an insight about it, listen closely because you will find ways in which you can apply aspects of their process to what you are working on.
Besides Eno's pioneering musical explorations in glam rock and later ambient works, few know that he actually developed a creativity tool in the '70s called Oblique Strategies. In 1975, Peter Schmidt and Brian Eno created the Oblique Strategy cards as a result of thinking about their creative process as artists. Eno has used the creativity tool throughout his career, most notably when producing David Bowie's 1977 album Heroes. You can order the creativity tool through his website.
In the new video below, Eno shares great insights on creativity and the fulfillment that can come from pioneering work.
"Distortion is character. In fact everything we call character, is the deviation from perfection. So, perfection to me is characterlessness."
Key Points
Doing one thing really well is ok
Everything good comes out of authentic enthusiasm
The big mistake is to wait for inspiration
Notice when something emerges that is new
Be a cowboy that goes out and finds new territory
Be ready to make use of opportunities that arise
Distortion is character and good
Perfection is characterlessness... So don't aim for it

title: brian eno taught me these 10 lessons in his music-making ...
text:
INTERVIEWS, REVIEWS & RELATED ARTICLES
MusicTech FEBRUARY 19, 2025 - by Garling Wu
BRIAN ENO TAUGHT ME THESE 10 LESSONS IN HIS MUSIC-MAKING WORKSHOP
Missed your chance to attend Brian Eno's class? Here are some key ideas to help anyone explore fresh ideas and methods for making music
At the start of 2025, I attended a series of workshops by Brian Eno, run by the School Of Song. Sharing his thoughts on creativity, studio methods, and plenty of personal anecdotes, it offered us a rare chance to hear from the master himself on a spectacular music career and a lifetime's worth of incredible musical advice.
Here are ten lessons I took away from the sessions - and which you can learn from, too.
BOREDOM IS IMPORTANT
"I'm almost sure that [Music For Airports] would have never happened had I not been sitting in an airport bored," says Eno - before adding, "and [being] slightly annoyed by German disco music".
It was perhaps a lot easier to be bored in the 1970s before the invention of the smartphone. These days, most of us spend hours avoiding being bored by scrolling through content platforms. "Consumerism is the fear of boredom embodied," Eno goes on to explain, but we need not be afraid of boredom. The next time you wake up, don't consume anything he suggests - not anything on your phone, not even your breakfast. Instead, see what enters your mind. "Something will appear," he says. For Eno, that 'something' planted the seed for one of his best-selling albums.
TAKING THINGS OUT IS AS IMPORTANT AS LEAVING THINGS IN
Challenging yourself to remove the main hook or riff in your song might seem self-defeating, but Eno thinks this is a powerful way to open up the rest of your mix and see the potential of each part.
There are two ways it can go: By removing the most important part, you might realise that none of the other instruments are doing much at all. On the other hand, as Eno explains, it might "make you realise that the least revolutionary part is the bit that you're hooked by".
One thing Eno would do at the end of every recording session is to create what he called the "film mix", that is in other words, taking the piece apart, leaving stuff out, and seeing if he could create something with the parts that were left.
PUSH THE LIMITS OF YOUR PARAMETERS
Eno believes that most of the truly interesting stuff happens at the outer limits. For any given parameter, he's more interested in what happens at the "edges of controls", than the comfortable middle range that most people stay in. After a lifetime of turning the knobs on all manner of studio gear, Eno says, "I've realised that the most interesting thing about controls is what happens at the extreme end of them".
TAKE NOTE OF WHAT GRABS YOUR ATTENTION
Creating good music starts by knowing what you like. At a time when algorithms vie for our attention, he repeatedly stressed the need to notice our thoughts and feelings. Eno often repeated the phrase, "If I do a double take, I do a triple take." In a production context, this means noticing when something feels off or identifying what really clicks - then asking yourself why.
BREAK THE GRID
Ignoring the gridlines in your DAW or opting for an unusual time signature are just some techniques Eno suggests for adding unpredictability to your work process.
It was something that he noticed while watching the young producer and his apprentice, Fred Again.., effortlessly navigate Logic Pro. Ignoring gridlines entirely, he would start by dropping sounds into the middle of the timeline.
"If you work in Logic and you're not a Fred, you tend to work in straight lines," Eno says, but what is key to Fred's music is that he ignored the boundaries that constrained most artists and acted more like a "collage artist", fluidly placing bits of music next to each other that completely ignored the grid.
CONSTRAINTS ARE GOOD
We've all felt the urge to buy more gear or invest in some sprawling software mega bundle, but Eno cautions against this. He believes limitations are something that drives our creative thinking and stops us from getting paralysed by endless options. "The kiss of death," warns Eno, "is software that says, 'Now you can do anything.'" In the digital age, self-imposed constraints are essential, says Eno, and goes so far as to suggest ideas like banning artificial reverb from the studio, forcing yourself to write a song in twenty minutes, flipping a coin to choose your chords or limiting the number of tracks in a session.
DOUBLE THE TEMPO
Alongside his pioneering avant-garde work, Eno has written plenty of chart toppers and produced some of the world's most famous bands. Along the way, he's picked up some recurring tricks that "nearly always make a song better".
One of these tricks he calls the Klaus Dinger beat, also known as the motorik beat. Named after the drummer from Neu!, it effectively doubles the tempo of a song. While working with U2 on Beautiful Day, Eno says the song wouldn't gel until he asked the band to try the Klaus Dinger beat. That simple repeating 4/4 beat gave the track momentum and turned it into the hit we know today.
NEVER DELETE ANYTHING
You might just find treasure in the trash, but the only guarantee you'll come across it is if you never empty the bin. That goes for your desktop bin too. According to Eno, he never gets rid of any idea, snippet, demo, or recording, reporting that he's got thousands of song ideas that he's collected over the years.
Over time, a well-kept archive becomes a creative library where you can pull out a recording on any given day and pick up where you left off. "I don't ever let anything go out of play, the point about the archive is to keep all the saucepans on the stove."
In the case that it's a total failure Eno will still stick to his rule, although he might leave his future self a reminder: "Sometimes I will give it a title like, 'Possibly the shittest piece of music I've ever done'."
FIND MUSIC IN EVERYDAY LIFE
While living in New York, Eno found himself fascinated with American radio. He would regularly record "shock jockeys" and shouting evangelists using a boom box and a cassette tape. Comparing American radio to the BBC back home, he thought, "This is amazing to live in such a fertile, unfiltered, sonic world."
This material eventually ended up in the album My Life In The Bush Of Ghosts with David Byrne. As he recalls, "I had recorded this guy off the radio... he was stuttering with nerves in a kind of fervent", that bit contrasted heavily with the host who replied rather flatly with: "Yeah, yeah yeah...". Taking these everyday recordings to the studio Eno pieced together the funky rhythmic track called America Is Waiting.
POLISH THE TURD
"Try to polish a turd," Eno suggests; it's one thing you can do with a piece of music you think is completely useless. It's an interesting take on a classic cliche.
According to Eno, what's great about something that's already bad is that there's no risk you can make it any worse and this frees you to try something utterly different. These bits that don't become a song on day one might continue to have a life in the future perhaps repurposed into a part for another song. Eno does this so often that he declares with a laugh, "I am probably one of the most prominent turd polishers in the business".
